newsitem.title: USA: Clinton gathers Arabs, Israeli for crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton gathers Arabs, Israeli for crisis talks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton gathered the leaders of Israel and the Palestinians in one room on Tuesday for a crisis summit designed to see "how far we can go" toward rescuing imperilled Middle East peace.

The White House Oval Office meeting among Clinton, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Jordan's King Hussein represented a U.S. effort to quell Middle East violence and rescue the peace process amid both high regional tensions and U.S. election year political pressures.
The initial group meeting broke up after about an hour and the four leaders strolled over to the White House residential area for lunch.

The White House said Clinton and the king later left, allowing Arafat and Netanyahu to continue two-way discussions, in what appeared a positive development. The aim of the summit was to bring the two feuding leaders together but there had been no guarantee they would hold private face-to-face talks.

U.S. politics intruded right at the outset of the planned two-day summit as Clinton's election rival, Bob Dole, issued a statement insisting the interests of "our friend Israel" be protected and the White House gave Dole a chilly brush-off.

Clinton got things rolling on Tuesday morning by talking separately with Netanyahu and Arafat, in that order, then gathered the whole group before a white marble fireplace in the Oval Office for joint discussions.
"We have had some good conversations already," he said, referring to his separate talks with Netanyahu and Arafat.
"Their presence here symbolises our commitment to end the violence and get the peace proces going again. What we're going to do is go to work, see how far we can go, see what we can produce."

The aim of Clinton's risky summit effort -- shunned by Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, who declined an invitation -- was to rescue a Middle East peace process in danger of collapsing after violence that killed 57 Palestinians and 15 Israelis in five days of violence last week.

It was only the second meeting between right-winger Netanyahu, 46, and Arafat, the 67-year-old former guerrilla chief who began fighting for Palestinian independence when he was a teenager in 1948, since the Israeli took office at the head of a hardline nationalist government last June.

A U.S. official said they shook hands and chatted briefly to break the ice before their talks in the Oval Office. Sensitive to Arab suspicions that this summit might add up to little more than such cosmetic touches the official added:
"While it is nice that it happened, we are looking for a lot more, obviously."

At the group meeting Netanyahu and Arafat faced each other from formal couches across an oval coffee table, with Clinton and King Hussein between them in stiff-backed chairs like a pair of referees. U.S. Vice President Al Gore sat next to Netanyahu and Secretary of State Warren Christopher next to Arafat.
The summit was proceeding under heavy security for Arafat and Netanyahu and under U.S.-imposed news controls that sought to minimise public statements and news media contacts.

Israeli officials nonetheless told reporters that Netanyahu's private meeting with Clinton was friendly and relaxed, with no U.S. attempt at arm-twisting. "There are no pressures," one said. "They talked about concrete issues."
But the heavy backdrop of U.S. election-year politics was immediately apparent as Netanyahu rearranged his schedule to include a meeting with Dole.

The meeting was initially arranged for late on Tuesday afternoon, but that diversion right in the middle of the summit raised some eyebrows and Dole's office later announced it had been postponed until late Wednesday afternoon.

Dole, far behind Clinton in opinion polls for the Nov. 5 election and edged into the shadows by this crisis, issued a statement on Monday saying, "Our friend Israel must not be asked to make concessions as a means of restoring order."
The White House dismissed his comment as "unnecessary."

"This president has provided extraordinary leadership in this region in the peace process precisely because we have fulfilled our commitment to our longtime ally Israel," spokesman Mike McCurry said."

Democrat Clinton needed to walk a diplomatic and political tightrope in hosting this summit, balancing neutrality among the contending Middle East parties with sensitivity for the outlook of American Jews, a potent U.S. voting bloc.
More tallks were planned on Wednesday at the White House and Blair House, an official guest house for distinguished foreign visitors just across Pennsylvania Avenue.

En route to Washington, Arafat told reporters he would attend the Washington summit with "no conditions or ultimatums." But there were unconfirmed reports in Israel that he had sent a letter to Clinton listing five demands.
For his part Netanyahu said he would propose immediate non-stop Israeli-Palestinian negotations to restart and round out peace plans begun with a celebrated accord in 1993.
